cards.front: Define "subsequence," "common subsequence," and "Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)" in the context of strings.
cards.back: A **subsequence** is a sequence that can be derived from another sequence by deleting zero or more elements without changing the order of the remaining elements. A **common subsequence** of two strings is a subsequence that is common to both strings. The **Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)** is the longest possible common subsequence among all common subsequences of the two strings.

cards.front: When finding the LCS of two strings, $S_1$ of length $m$ and $S_2$ of length $n$, what are the two main cases to consider when comparing their last characters, $S_1[m-1]$ and $S_2[n-1]$?
cards.back:
The two main cases are:
1.  **If $S_1[m-1] == S_2[n-1]$**: The last characters match. This character must be part of the LCS. The problem reduces to finding the LCS of the prefixes $S_1[0...m-2]$ and $S_2[0...n-2]$, and adding 1 to its length.
2.  **If $S_1[m-1] \neq S_2[n-1]$**: The last characters do not match. The LCS cannot include both $S_1[m-1]$ and $S_2[n-1]$. The problem reduces to taking the maximum of two subproblems: LCS of $S_1[0...m-2]$ and $S_2[0...n-1]$, OR LCS of $S_1[0...m-1]$ and $S_2[0...n-2]$.

cards.front: Derive the recurrence relation for the length of the Longest Common Subsequence, $LCS(S_1[0...m-1], S_2[0...n-1])$.
cards.back:
Let $LCS(i, j)$ denote the length of the LCS of prefixes $S_1[0...i-1]$ and $S_2[0...j-1]$.

$$ LCS(i, j) = \begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } i=0 \text{ or } j=0 \\
1 + LCS(i-1, j-1) & \text{if } S_1[i-1] == S_2[j-1] \\
\max(LCS(i-1, j), LCS(i, j-1)) & \text{if } S_1[i-1] \neq S_2[j-1]
\end{cases} $$

cards.front: What are the base cases for the LCS recurrence relation, $LCS(S_1[0...m-1], S_2[0...n-1])$?
cards.back:
The base cases occur when one or both of the input strings (or their prefixes) are empty. Specifically:
*   If $m=0$ (the first string is empty), $LCS(0, n) = 0$.
*   If $n=0$ (the second string is empty), $LCS(m, 0) = 0$.

This means if either $i$ or $j$ is 0 in $LCS(i, j)$, the length of the common subsequence is 0.

cards.front: In the standard dynamic programming approach for LCS, what does $dp[i][j]$ represent, and in what order is the $dp$ table typically filled?
cards.back:
The cell $dp[i][j]$ typically represents the length of the Longest Common Subsequence of the first $i$ characters of string $S_1$ ($S_1[0...i-1]$) and the first $j$ characters of string $S_2$ ($S_2[0...j-1]$).

The $dp$ table is typically filled in a bottom-up manner, iterating through rows and columns. This means cells are computed from top-left to bottom-right, ensuring that all required subproblem solutions ($dp[i-1][j-1]$, $dp[i-1][j]$, $dp[i][j-1]$) are available before computing $dp[i][j]$.

cards.front: State the time and space complexities of the standard dynamic programming algorithm for finding the length of the LCS of two strings of lengths $m$ and $n$.
cards.back:
The standard DP algorithm for LCS has:
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(mn)$. This is because a 2D $m \times n$ DP table is constructed, and each cell takes constant time to compute based on previously computed cells.
*   **Space Complexity:** $O(mn)$. This is due to storing the $m \times n$ DP table. (Note: Space can be optimized to $O(\min(m, n))$ by only storing the current and previous rows/columns, but $O(mn)$ is standard for reconstruction).

cards.front: Describe the general approach to reconstruct one of the actual LCS strings from the filled $dp$ table, after computing its length.
cards.back:
To reconstruct an LCS, start from the bottom-right cell $dp[m][n]$ and backtrack:
1.  If $S_1[i-1] == S_2[j-1]$: The characters match. This character is part of the LCS. Append $S_1[i-1]$ (or $S_2[j-1]$) to the result and move diagonally up-left to $dp[i-1][j-1]$.
2.  If $S_1[i-1] \neq S_2[j-1]$: The characters don't match. Move to the cell (either $dp[i-1][j]$ or $dp[i][j-1]$) that has the larger value. If they are equal, either path works. This indicates we're moving away from a character that wasn't part of the LCS. Continue until $i=0$ or $j=0$. The reconstructed string will be in reverse order, so it needs to be reversed.

cards.front: Given $S_1 = \text{"ABCBDAB"}$ and $S_2 = \text{"BDCABA"}$, what is the length of their Longest Common Subsequence?
cards.back:
The length of the Longest Common Subsequence for $S_1 = \text{"ABCBDAB"}$ and $S_2 = \text{"BDCABA"}$ is $\mathbf{4}$.

Examples of LCS include "BCBA", "BDAB", "BCAB".
